parole.significato: The act of abandoning, or the state of being abandoned; total desertion; relinquishment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French abandonnement, from abandonner (“to abandon, relinquish”). abandonner was originally equivalent to mettre à bandon (“to leave to the jurisdiction, i.e. of another”), bandon being from Medieval Latin bandum, bannum (“order, decree, ban”). Equivalent to abandon + -ment. (See also

parole.significato: The act of abrading, wearing, or rubbing off; the wearing away by friction.
parole.testo: First attested in 1656. From French abrasion (attested since 1611), from Medieval Latin abrasio (“a scraping”), from Latin abrādō (“scrape off”). See also abrade.

parole.significato: The process of adapting something or becoming adapted to a situation; adjustment, modification.
parole.testo: From French adaptation, from Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptō (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”); see adapt. Equivalent to adapt + -ation.

parole.significato: Sticky; tenacious, as glutinous substances.
parole.testo: From French adhésif, from Medieval Latin adhaesivus, from adhaereō (supine adhaesum); see adhere.

parole.significato: Characterized by admiration.
parole.testo: Via French admiratif or directly from its etymon, Medieval Latin admirativus.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being affined; mental affinity or attraction.
parole.testo: From French affiner, from Medieval Latin affinare, affine + -ition.

parole.significato: An early chemical apparatus, consisting of two retorts connected by a tube, used to purify substances by distillation.
parole.testo: From French alambic, from Medieval Latin alembīcus, from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Doublet of ambix and lambic.

parole.significato: One of a class of caustic bases, such as soda, soda ash, caustic soda, potash, ammonia, and lithia, whose distinguishin…
parole.testo: From French alcali, from Medieval Latin alcali, ultimately from Arabic اَلْقِلْي (al-qily, “alkali, ashes (in reference to ashes of the saltwort)”), related to قَلَى (qalā, “to roast in a pan, fry”).

parole.significato: A small circle on the celestial sphere, parallel to the horizon, that is used in astronomy and navigation to show altit…
parole.testo: From Middle English almicanteras, French almicantarat, almucantarat, from Medieval Latin almicantarath, almucantarath, from Arabic المقنطرات (almuqanṭarāt, “circles of celestial latitude”), from قَنْطَرَة (qanṭara, “arch”).

parole.significato: An almond-shaped inclusion in igneous rock or lava.
parole.testo: From French amygdale, from Medieval Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”). Doublet of almond, amygdala, and mandorla.

parole.significato: A right to receive amounts of money regularly over a certain fixed period, in perpetuity, or, especially, over the rema…
parole.testo: From French annuité, from Medieval Latin annuitās, from Latin annuus (“annual”). Cf. annuality.

parole.significato: A devotional chant; a piece of music sung responsively.
parole.testo: From French antiphone or Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”), neuter plural substantive of ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “concordant”) from ἀντί (antí, “in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Doublet of anthem.

parole.significato: A short, witty, instructive saying; an aphorism or maxim.
parole.testo: From French apophthegme or Medieval Latin apothegma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφθεγμα (apóphthegma), from ἀποφθέγγομαι (apophthéngomai, “speak out”).

parole.significato: One of the aristocracy, nobility, or people of rank in a community; one of a ruling class; a noble (originally in Revol…
parole.testo: From French aristocrate (“aristocrat”), attested once in the 16th century but recoined in the Revolutionary era, from aristocratie (“aristocracy”), from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aristokratía), from ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) (compare Old English ar) + κράτος (krát

parole.significato: A ceremonial pointed knife or dagger, used especially in Wicca and other neopagan traditions and typically having a bla…
parole.testo: From French athamé in a 1929 passage from É.-J. Grillot de Givry (see 1931 citation below), apparently from Medieval Latin artavus (“quill-sharpening knife”). Artavus was also mistranslated into artauo in an Italian manuscript. The arthame was conflated with the cortel nero (“black knife”) by Grillo

parole.significato: A bachelor's degree.
parole.testo: First attested in 1625; borrowed from French baccalauréat, from Medieval Latin baccalaureātus, from Medieval Latin baccalaureus, an alteration made to baccalārius (“young man aspiring to knighthood, apprentice, bachelor”) for it to resemble bacca lauri (“laurel berry”) (the ancient symbol of victory

parole.significato: Common in a boring way, to the point of being predictable; containing nothing new or fresh.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French banal (“held in common, relating to feudal service, by extension commonplace”), from Old French banel, related to Medieval Latin bannālis (“subject to feudal authority”), from Latin bannus (“jurisdiction”), both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (“to order, summon, forbid”

parole.significato: To make blissful.
parole.testo: From French béatifier, from Medieval Latin beātifico (“I bless”).

parole.significato: Any of very many evergreen or deciduous shrubs of the genus Berberis.
parole.testo: From the genus name Berberis, from French berbère, from Medieval Latin barberis, from Arabic بَرْبَارِيس (barbārīs). Doublet of barberry and related to Berber.

parole.significato: A sort of fine buckram.
parole.testo: From French bocassin, boucassin, from Old French boucacin, boucassin, from Medieval Latin bocassinus, from Old Anatolian Turkish بوغاسی (boğası).

parole.significato: A putative, secret organization of individuals gathered for a political purpose.
parole.testo: From French cabale, from Medieval Latin cabbala, which in turn is derived from Hebrew קַבָּלָה (kabalá, “Jewish mysticism”, literally “reception, something received”) (such as knowledge). Doublet of Kabbalah, as well as, more distantly, ghibli.

parole.significato: To persuade someone to do something which they are reluctant to do, especially by flattery or promises; to coax.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cajoler, probably a blend of Middle French cageoler (“chatter like a jay”) (from gajole, dialectal diminutive of geai (“jaybird”)) + Old French gaioler (“entice into a cage”), which is from Medieval Latin gabiola, from Late Latin caveola (whence English caveola), diminutive of L

parole.significato: Synonym of smithsonite, a pink form of zinc oxide (mainly zinc carbonate ZnCO₃) formed as a byproduct of zinc sublimati…
parole.testo: From French calamine, from Medieval Latin calamīna, from Latin cadmīa, ultimately from Ancient Greek Κᾰδμείᾱ (Kădmeíā), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”). Doublet of cadmia, calaminaris, and lapis calaminaris.

parole.significato: Carline thistle (Carlina spp.).
parole.testo: From French carline, from Medieval Latin carlina, probably from cardina, a diminutive of Latin carduus (“thistle”), with influence from Carolus Magnus due to an association with Charlemagne.

parole.significato: A purplish-red pigment, made from dye obtained from the cochineal beetle; carminic acid or any of its derivatives.
parole.testo: PIE word  *kʷŕ̥mis Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *kʷŕ̥mis Proto-Indo-Iranian *kŕ̥miš Persian کرمست* (*kermest)bor. Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz)bor. Medieval Latin *carminium? parole.significato: Relating to censive tenure; held in return for the payment of a cens (a feudal rent).
parole.testo: Borrowed from French censive, from Medieval Latin censivus; compare English census.

parole.significato: The mistress of a castle or large household.
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from French châtelaine, the feminine form of châtelain (“castle-keeper, castellan; one living in a castle”), from Medieval Latin castellanus (“occupants of a castle”), from castellum (“castle, fort”) (diminutive of castrum (“castle, fort”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱes- (“to cut off, sep

parole.significato: A glass covering, originally bell-shaped, for garden plants to prevent frost damage and promote early growth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cloche (“bell”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”). Doublet of cloak and clock.

parole.significato: A brandy distilled from white wine in the region around Cognac in France.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French cognac, from Cognac, a city in France, from Medieval Latin Comniacum, from the name Cominius + Gallo-Roman suffix -acum, from Proto-Celtic *-ākom.

parole.significato: To occupy exactly the same space.
parole.testo: From French coïncider, from Medieval Latin coincidere, from con- + incidere, from in- (“into, to”) + cadere (“to fall, fall down, drop”).

parole.significato: Of two or more objects: being in the same location.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from French coïncident, from Medieval Latin coincidentem, an accusative singular form of Latin coincidēns (“coinciding”), the present active participle of coincidō (“to coincide”), from co- (variant of con- (prefix denoting a being or bringing together of several objects))

parole.significato: An employee of a hotel who attends to the requirements and wishes of guests.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concierge (“caretaker; doorkeeper; lodge-keeper of a château”), from Old French conciarge, consierge, consirge, from Medieval Latin consergius; further etymology uncertain, probably from Vulgar Latin *cōnservius, from Latin cōnservus (“fellow servant; fellow slave”), from con- (

parole.significato: Following, in succession, without interruption.
parole.testo: From French consécutif, from Medieval Latin cōnsecūtīvus, from Latin cōnsecūtus (“followed up”), from Latin cōnsequor (“to travel”).

parole.significato: The quality or fact of having a physical or material body.
parole.testo: From French corporéité or Medieval Latin corporeitas, from Latin corporeus, from corpus (“body”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a rib.
parole.testo: From French costal and its etymon Medieval Latin costālis, from Latin costa (“rib”). As a Spanish unit, via Spanish costal. By surface analysis, costa + -al. Piecewise doublet of coastal.

parole.significato: A circle of individuals who associate with one another for a common purpose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coterie.

parole.significato: A reputation impacting one's ability to be believed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French crédibilité, from Medieval Latin credibilitas, from Latin credibilis. By surface analysis, credible + -ity.

parole.significato: Any of the Papally-endorsed military expeditions undertaken by the Christians of Latin Europe in the 11th to 13th centu…
parole.testo: From French croisade, introduced into English (in the French spelling) by 1575. The modern spelling emerges c. 1760,. parole.significato: A small circular receptacle used in assaying gold or silver with lead.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French coupelle, from Medieval Latin cūpella, from Latin cūpa (“cask”) + -ella (“-elle: forming feminine diminutives”). Equivalent to cup + -el.

parole.significato: A container in which a sacred object is kept; a pyx.
parole.testo: From French custode (“pyx”), from Medieval Latin custōdia. Doublet of custody.

parole.significato: A state of moral or artistic decline or deterioration; decay
parole.testo: From French décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia (“decay”), from *decadens (“decaying”), present participle of *decadere (“to decay”); see decay.

parole.significato: Characterized by moral or cultural decline.
parole.testo: From French décadent, a back-formation from décadence (see -ent), from Medieval Latin dēcadentia, from Late Latin dēcadēns, present participle of dēcadō, dēcidō (“sink, fall; perish”), from Latin dē- + cadō (“fall”).

parole.significato: To pour off (a liquid) gently, so as not to disturb the sediment.
parole.testo: From French décanter, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).

parole.significato: A storage facility, in particular, a warehouse.
parole.testo: From French dépôt, from Old French depost, from Medieval Latin dēpositum, from Latin, participle of dēpōnō, dēpōnere. Doublet of deposit.

parole.significato: Causing depression; dispiriting.
parole.testo: From French dépressif or Medieval Latin depressivus. By surface analysis, depress + -ive.

parole.significato: To sell at a reduced price.
parole.testo: Alteration of French descompte, décompte, from Old French disconter, desconter (“reckon off, account back, discount”), from Medieval Latin discomputō (“to deduct, discount”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + computō (“to reckon, count”). By surface analysis, dis- + count.

parole.significato: To disculpate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1602; borrowed from French disculper or its own etymon, Medieval Latin disculpō, from dis- + culpō. Doublet of disculpate.

parole.significato: An administrative division of an area.
parole.testo: From French district, from Medieval Latin districtus (“a district within which the lord may distrain, also jurisdiction”), from Latin districtus, past participle of distringere (“to draw asunder, compel, distrain”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringere (“to draw tight, strain”). Doublet of Detroit.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a domain.
parole.testo: From French domanial, from Medieval Latin domanialis, from Latin dominium + -alis.

parole.significato: A person who legally resides in a particular place.
parole.testo: From French domiciliaire, from Medieval Latin domiciliārius, from Latin domicilium (“dwelling”).

parole.significato: A tile divided into two squares, each having 0 to 6 (or sometimes more) dots or pips (as in dice), used in the game of…
parole.testo: 1801, borrowed from French domino (1771), originally the term for a hooded garment, itself from Medieval Latin domino, oblique case of dominus (“lord, master”); compare Medieval Latin dominicale (“a kind of veil”). By surface analysis, di- + -omino.

parole.significato: Synonym of brandy.
parole.testo: From French eau-de-vie (“water of life”), calque of Medieval Latin aqua vītae. Compare akvavit, aquavit, aqua vitae, whisky, whiskey, and water of life from the same source.

parole.significato: A widespread disease that affects many humans in a population.
parole.testo: From French épidémique, from épidémie, from Medieval Latin epidēmia, reanalysis of plural Late Latin epidēmia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιδήμιος (epidḗmios), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”). By surface analysis, epi- (“on”) + demic (“of the people”).

parole.significato: The condition of being equivalent or essentially equal: the status of being interchangeable.
parole.testo: From French équivalence, from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

parole.significato: Excessive or superfluous expenditure of money.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French extravagance, from Medieval Latin extra + vagor (“to wander”).

parole.significato: A kind of coarse woollen cloth or stuff with a shaggy or tufted (friezed) nap on one side.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships. Or, from French friser (“to curl”)..

parole.significato: A male waiter (especially at a French restaurant).
parole.testo: From French garçon m (1788), from Old French garçon, oblique case of gars (“servant”), from Medieval Latin garciō m, from Frankish *wrakkjō (“servant, boy”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, driven one”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to drive”). Cognate with Old High German wrecheo, recko (

parole.significato: The discipline which deals with the measurement and representation of Earth, its gravitational field and geodynamic phe…
parole.testo: From French géodésie, from Medieval Latin geōdaesia, from Ancient Greek γεωδαισία (geōdaisía), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + δαίω (daíō, “to divide”). By surface analysis, geode + -esy.

parole.significato: Roughly spherical in shape; globe-shaped.
parole.testo: From French globulaire or Medieval Latin globulāris.

parole.significato: A teacher of prose literature and letters in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From French grammatiste, from the Medieval Latin grammatista, from the Ancient Greek γραμματιστής (grammatistḗs), from γράμμα (grámma, “letter”).

parole.significato: A grid of horizontal and vertical lines; specifically, one used as a guide to proportionately enlarge or reduce a drawi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French graticule, from Medieval Latin grātīcula, from Latin crāticula (“grating, grill”), from crātis (“hurdle; wickerwork”) (probably from Proto-Indo-European *kréh₂-tis (“fenced handiwork”)) + -cula (feminine form of -culus, a variant of -ulus (“diminutive suffix”)).

parole.significato: The state of being grateful.
parole.testo: From French gratitude, from Medieval Latin grātitūdō (“thankfulness”), from Latin grātus (“thankful”). Displaced Old English þancung.

parole.significato: A hard yellow cheese originating from Gruyères, Switzerland and made in the cantons of Fribourg.
parole.testo: (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “the Medieval Latin name's origins need explanation”) Named after the town of Gruyères, Switzerland, from Medieval Latin Gruerius, from Swiss French grue (“crane”).

parole.significato: A wandering monk having no fixed monastery, as exemplified in the Rule of St. Benedict.
parole.testo: Early 19th century, borrowed from French gyrovague, from Medieval Latin gȳrovagus (“wandering aimlessly”).

parole.significato: One who destroys religious images or icons, especially an opponent of the Orthodox Church in the 8th and 9th centuries,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French iconoclaste and its etymon Medieval Latin īconoclastēs, from Byzantine Greek εἰκονοκλάστης (eikonoklástēs, literally “image breaker”). By surface analysis, icono- + -clast.

parole.significato: Identical.
parole.testo: From French identique, from Medieval Latin identicus (“the same”), from Latin identi-, from idem (“the same”).

parole.significato: To establish the identity of someone or something.
parole.testo: From French identifier, from Medieval Latin identicus + Latin faciō.

parole.significato: Contrary to, forbidden, or not authorized by law, especially criminal law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French illégal, from Medieval Latin illegalis, from Latin legalis, by surface analysis, il- + legal. In senses relating to immigration, via clipping of illegal alien or illegal immigrant.

parole.significato: Serving to initiate.
parole.testo: From French initiative, from Medieval Latin *initiativus (“serving to initiate”), from Late Latin initiare (“to begin, to initiate”), from Latin initium (“beginning”), from ineo (“enter, begin”). By surface analysis, initiate + -ive.

parole.significato: The rise and fall of the voice in speaking.
parole.testo: From French intonation, from Medieval Latin intonatio, from intonō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Any of several insects of the genus Kermes.
parole.testo: PIE word  *kʷŕ̥mis First attested ca. 1600, from French kermès, from Medieval Latin cremesinus (compare Italian chermes, Spanish carmes), from Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz) (whence also Portuguese quermes, alquermes), from a Persian word meaning “worm-colored” (compare modern Persian قرمز (qermez)), ultim

parole.significato: A building used to house lepers, usually in permanent quarantine from the rest of society.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French léproserie and léprosarie, from Medieval Latin leprōsārium, from leprōsus (“leprous”) + -ārium (“-ary: building related to”). Equivalent to leprose + -ery.

parole.significato: The metric unit of fluid measure, equal to one cubic decimetre. Symbol: L, l, or ℓ.
parole.testo: From French litre, from Medieval Latin litra, from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “a Sicilian coin, a measure of weight”). Related to Latin lībra. Doublet of arratel, libbra, Libra, libra, lira, litra, livre, and rottol.

parole.significato: A dry red or white burgundy wine produced around Mâcon or extremely similar to such wines.
parole.testo: An anglicized form of French Mâcon, from earlier Mascon and Medieval Latin Masconis, a syncopated form of Madasconis and Matisco, probably from Gaulish matus (“bear”) and a suffix equivalent to -iscus (“-ish: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: A type of herb referred to by Pliny as "asyla"; potentially chickweed or ivy-leaved speedwell.
parole.testo: First attested in 1572. Borrowed from French morgeline, derived from Medieval Latin Morsus gallinae. See also chickweed, henbit.

parole.significato: A heavy crepe fabric of silk, wool, or both, having a cross-ribbed texture, used for apparel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French marocain (“Moroccan”), from Maroc (“Morocco”) (from Medieval Latin Marrochium (“the city of Marrakech, the former capital of Morocco”)) + -ain (suffix forming demonyms).

parole.significato: Synonym of Macon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Mascon, from Medieval Latin Masconis, a syncopated form of Madasconis and Matisco, probably from Gaulish matus (“bear”) (from Proto-Celtic *matus, commonly understood as a euphemistic derivation from *matis (“good”)) and a suffix equivalent to -iscus (“-ish: forming adjectives”)

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the practice of medicine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French médical, from Medieval Latin medicālis, from Latin medicus. Replaced Old English lǣċe (“doctor (physician)”), which is cognate with Icelandic læknir (“doctor”).

parole.significato: An aubergine; an eggplant.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French mélongène, from Medieval Latin melongena, Italian melanzana, from Greek μελιτζάνα (melitzána), from Arabic اَلْبَاذِنْجَان (al-bāḏinjān, “eggplant”), from Classical Persian بادنگان (bādingān), from باتنگان (bātingān), from Sanskrit वातिगगम (vātiga-gama, “eggplant”). Doublet of a

parole.significato: A small bit; a morsel or snippet.
parole.testo: From French morceau, from Old French morsel, from Medieval Latin morsellum (“a bit, a little piece”), diminutive of Latin morsum (“a bit”), neuter of morsus, past participle of mordeō, mordēre (“bite, nibble, gnaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to rub, wipe; to pack, rob”). Doublet of morse

parole.significato: The principle that a person (particularly a refugee) should not be returned to an area (chiefly their country of origin…
parole.testo: From non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + refoulement. Refoulement is borrowed from French refoulement (“act of pushing something back (as gunpowder into a gun barrel, or water by a dam); act of water overflowing; forced relocation of a group of people; forced repatriation of asylum-seekers or refugees”),

parole.significato: Oily, greasy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French oléagineux, borrowed from Medieval Latin oleāginōsus (“oily”), from olea (“the olive tree or its fruit”).

parole.significato: Nerium oleander, a notoriously poisonous shrub in the dogbane family, Apocynaceae, but nonetheless widely grown as an o…
parole.testo: From French oléandre, from Medieval Latin oleandru, from Late Latin lorandrum, perhaps an alteration of rhododendron.

parole.significato: A royal charter confirming to a subject all his possessions.
parole.testo: From French, from Medieval Latin pancharta. See pan- and carte.

parole.significato: Relative to a period or periods.
parole.testo: From French périodique, from Medieval Latin periodicus (“cyclical”), from Latin periodus (“complete sentence, period, circuit”), from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “cycle, period of time”). By surface analysis, period + -ic.

parole.significato: A fluid consisting of a mixture of refined petroleum hydrocarbons, primarily consisting of octane, commonly used as a m…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French (essence de) pétrole, from Medieval Latin petroleum, from Ancient Greek πετρέλαιον (petrélaion, “oil of the rock”), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”)+ ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil, any oily substance”). Doublet of petroleum.

parole.significato: Advertising or other activity designed to rouse public interest in something.
parole.testo: From French publicité, From Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, accusative singular of pūblicitās, from Latin pūblicus (“public, general”). Morphologically public + -ity.

parole.significato: The state of being actual or real; realness.
parole.testo: From French réalité (“quality of being real”), from Middle French realité (“property, possession”), from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), equivalent to real + -ity. Recorded since 1550 as a legal term in the sense of “fixed property” (compare real estate, realty); the sense

parole.significato: The involuntary sending of refugees or asylum seekers to their country of origin or another one, where they are likely…

parole.significato: Synonym of result.
parole.testo: From French resultat (now résultat), from Medieval Latin resultātum.

parole.significato: A table or shelf behind an altar, on which are placed images or holy objects.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French retable, ultimately from Medieval Latin retrotabulum.

parole.significato: A character or part played by a performer or actor.
parole.testo: From French rôle, from Middle French rolle, from Old French role, from Medieval Latin rotulus. Doublet of roll and rotulus.

parole.significato: A cyclist who performs well on flat and undulating roads.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French rouleur (“one who causes something to roll, roller; something which rolls; cyclist who performs well on flat and undulating roads, rouleur”), from rouler (“to roll”) + -eur (suffix forming masculine nouns from verbs). Rouler is derived from Old French ruele, roele (“small wheel”

parole.significato: Any vegetable of certain species in the onion family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French échalote, from Middle French eschalote, alteration of Old French eschaloigne, from Medieval Latin escalonia, from Latin ascalonia (cēpa) (“onion of Ashkelon”). Doublet of scallion.

parole.significato: Having traits or characteristics in common; alike, allied, comparable.
